sentences.text: The ringing station where Tamar's father worked was in a shallow valley in the Negev desert, three hours south of Tel Aviv, on a small dirt road that ended at the door.
It was really just one long building — a stone base with a corrugated tin roof, with a kitchen at one end and a lab at the other and a couple of small bunks in between.
Around it, in every direction, was pale bone-colored desert with low grey hills at the edges of the sky.
There was almost nothing there.
That was the point.
It was almost nothing there that made the birds visible.

Every autumn, when the northern hemisphere started to cool, hundreds of millions of small birds — warblers and flycatchers and shrikes and every kind of songbird — flew from Europe and western Asia south into Africa for the winter.
The route took most of them across Israel.
The Negev was one of the last stopping places they had before the Sinai desert and then the long crossing of the Red Sea.
So they stopped, and rested, and ate, in the wadi behind the station.

And Tamar's father and his small team put up mist nets — very fine soft nets, hard to see even up close — and gently caught a tiny handful of the birds each day, and put a small silver band on one leg, and let them go.
Tamar had visited the station many times, from the time she was small.
But this year was different.
This year she was eleven, and her father had said she could stay for the last two weeks of the autumn ringing season and actually help.
Not just watch — actually help.
Empty the nets.
Hold the birds.
Learn to identify them.
She had wanted this for as long as she could remember.
She had gone out into the field with the assistants the previous summer, but only to carry things.
This year she got to work.
Her father was a serious quiet man.
Around her mother, he sometimes joked.
In the field, he did not joke.
His whole face and voice changed when he was working.
He was not less kind, but he was — Tamar had noticed — completely focused, in a way that felt almost like a different person.
On the first morning at the station, over coffee at dawn, before they went out, he said, "You will be careful.
You will do exactly what I show you.
If I say stop, you stop.
A wild bird in your hand is a very fragile thing.
You cannot practice on them.
You have to be right the first time.
Are you ready." Tamar nodded.
She was ready.
They walked out to the nets.
It was still nearly dark.
There were five nets, each strung between two tall poles about four meters apart.
The nets were made of very fine soft mesh, and in the pale dawn light they were almost invisible.
Her father walked slowly along the line, looking.
Tamar walked beside him.
"Bird," he said quietly, at the second net.
Tamar looked.
A tiny warm brown shape was caught in the middle of the mesh, hanging quietly, its little feet gripping a strand.
Her father reached in with very careful hands.
He worked the bird out of the net.
It was so small — the size of a plum.
He held it in his cupped hands.
He turned to Tamar.
"Willow warbler," he said.
"See the pale legs?
See the little eyebrow stripe?
Come on.
Back to the lab."
In the lab, her father showed her how to hold the bird — with the head between the index and middle fingers of one hand, with the body cradled softly in the palm.
He weighed it.
He measured its wing.
He noted its fat and its molt.
Then he took a very small ring from a numbered strip and, using a special pair of pliers, he closed it gently around one thin leg.
"Every ring has a unique number," he said.
"If this bird is ever caught again — anywhere, by anyone — the number tells us who it is.
Where it came from.
Where it went."
Then he handed the bird to Tamar.
Very carefully.
He showed her the grip.
She held it.
The warbler was so light that she could barely feel it.
It was warm.
Its heart was beating very fast against her fingers.
It looked at her — one tiny black eye.
"Now," her father said.
"Go outside.
Hold it up over your head.
Open your fingers, don't throw it.
Just let it go." So Tamar went outside.
She held the little bird up.
She opened her hand.
And the bird did not fly at first — it sat on her palm for one long second, deciding, and then it burst up into the pale desert sky and was gone.
Tamar watched it go.
She stood there for a long moment.
She had done this.
She had let a wild bird fly.
For the first four days she and her father worked the nets.
Every morning they got up at four.
Every morning they walked the line.
They caught, on some days, five or six birds.
On other days, only one or two.
They ringed each one.
They released each one.
Tamar learned to tell a Sardinian warbler from a Cyprus warbler, and a common redstart from a black redstart, and a lesser whitethroat from every other whitethroat.
By the fourth day her father let her check a net alone.
And on the fifth morning, at the first net, she found the bird her father had been waiting for.
